summary: The evidence is still thin. All 14 openings are cover only again: 10 are last week's videos and 4 are new, and none had their spoken words transcribed, so we have titles and covers but no real first seconds. The covers that broke out share three things. They show one clear idea in a single line, they put a face or character reacting beside it, and they either name a frustration the viewer already has or flatly contradict what the viewer believes. The new arrivals add three structures that fit Flowra well: getting a result without the usual chore, sorting a messy pile of work by impact, and two numbers shown side by side.

patterns.name: Still stuck, now simple
patterns.formula: You still can't [do the thing you keep putting off]. Now it takes [one small, concrete step].
patterns.why: The first line names a frustration the viewer already has, so they recognise themselves straight away. The second line promises relief, so staying feels worth it.
patterns.picture: A reacting face (wide eyes, finger pointing at the text) beside the stuck task, then the easy version appears. For Floey: she points at a wilting flower and it lights up as 'found'.
patterns.forFlowra: Your pages losing clicks are already in Search Console. Flowra lines them up.

examples.words: Cover text (Hindi): 'Still can't make AI videos? Now making AI video is this easy! Just 2 simple steps'
examples.onScreen: Cover only: surprised young man pointing at the headline, an AI icon and a video thumbnail

examples.words: Cover text: 'How to create AI product review videos. Step-by-step full tutorial!'
examples.onScreen: Cover only: woman pointing at product screenshots, 'BEST DEAL!' badge

patterns.name: Good news with a catch
patterns.formula: Your [gain you wanted] means nothing until you [check the thing you skipped].
patterns.why: It opens on something the viewer wants and then takes it away, so they stay to hear the catch. Our house rules turn the original yes or no question into a statement.
patterns.picture: A person or character watching something rise, then one warning word appears on screen. For Floey: a flower blooms, then she looks over the whole garden to see whether every flower grew.
patterns.forFlowra: Your traffic jump proves nothing until you compare it with the whole site.

examples.words: Title: 'More visitors = more opportunities! But can your website handle the traffic?' On screen: 'hosting'
examples.onScreen: Cover only: man at a laptop by a city window, glowing data, one red word 'hosting'

patterns.name: The animated action
patterns.formula: [Character] does [one physical action] while you hear what [the product] does for you.
patterns.why: Motion in the first frame, like a fist slamming a glowing button, catches the eye before any words land. An animated character also tells the viewer straight away that this is not a person reading an ad.
patterns.picture: An animated character in the middle of an action in the very first frame, with no title card. For Floey: she dives straight onto a wilting flower and starts trimming one petal.
patterns.forFlowra: Your rewrite keeps what works and changes only the sections that slipped.

examples.words: Title: 'JOOUZSEO – AI-Powered SEO Content Automation | Create, Rank & Scale Faster'
examples.onScreen: Cover only: 3D animated man in a suit slamming a glowing button, blue cloud behind

patterns.name: The flat contradiction
patterns.formula: [The thing your field swears by] doesn't [do what you think]. [The overlooked thing] does.
patterns.why: A short, confident claim against what the viewer believes creates an itch that only the explanation can scratch. It also takes under two seconds to say.
patterns.picture: A character mid-expression, with the word being challenged repeated or crossed out around them. For Floey: she flies past a shiny new flower to a drooping old one.
patterns.forFlowra: Publishing more won't fix your traffic. The pages already losing clicks will.

examples.onScreen: Cover only: animated bald character laughing, the word 'BLANK' scattered all around him

examples.words: Title: 'YouTube SEO Method That Actually Works'
examples.onScreen: Cover only: woman with a raised finger, 'YOUTUBE SEO FOR MORE VIEWS!' and a rising bar chart

patterns.name: The brutal report card
patterns.formula: Your [thing] just got [a harsh review], and [the part that failed] is [specific].
patterns.why: Being judged is uncomfortable and funny at the same time, so viewers stay to hear the verdict. A big emotional caption tells them how to feel before the details arrive.
patterns.picture: A character reacting to a written report, with a large reaction caption. For Floey: she holds a tiny report card over a row of flowers, and the oldest ones droop.
patterns.forFlowra: Your blog just got its report card, and the oldest flowers are failing.

examples.words: On screen: 'THIS IS VERY HURTFUL' (title: 'WARDOGS AI Gave Peanut a BRUTAL Performance Review...')
examples.onScreen: Cover only: game characters over a text report card, a huge yellow and white caption

patterns.name: The screenshot receipt
patterns.formula: Your [tool or chart you trust] shows [the movement]. It won't show you [the cause].
patterns.why: A familiar interface or a sharply moving line in the first frame is readable in a split second and makes the claim believable before the viewer can doubt it. Saying what the screen hides creates a gap the reel then fills. This pattern now also covers last week's 'chart in frame one'.
patterns.picture: A real-looking results screen or dashboard line fills the frame, with one line highlighted or one sharp turn labelled, and a face or character reacting. For Floey: the garden's single total line dips, then she zooms down to the one flower that caused it. Show only the shape, never a made-up figure.
patterns.forFlowra: Your traffic chart shows the drop. It won't tell you which page caused it.

examples.onScreen: Cover only: two Google AI Overview results side by side, a reaction face below

patterns.name: Without the usual chore
patterns.formula: You can [get the result] without [the tedious step everyone assumes you need].
patterns.why: It removes a step the viewer dreads, so the promise feels personal and immediate. Talking calmly to camera with one short caption makes it feel like a tip from a friend, not an ad.
patterns.picture: A calm face or character looking straight at the viewer, with one short caption (even a single word) at the bottom. For Floey: she hovers facing the camera while a stack of spreadsheets behind her blows away.
patterns.forFlowra: You can find your fading pages without exporting a single spreadsheet.

examples.words: On screen: 'Free.' (title: 'Bulk Google Index Checker (Google, Bing, Yandex) | SpeedyIndex')
examples.onScreen: Cover only: woman smiling straight into the camera, small brand logo at the top, one-word caption 'Free.'

examples.words: On screen: 'We index any third-party URLs.' (title: 'How to Index Backlinks Without Search Console')
examples.onScreen: Cover only: woman holding a fluffy mic, speaking to camera in a bright room, one-line caption

patterns.name: The pile, sorted
patterns.formula: Your next [win] is already in [the pile you have]. [Sort it by impact].
patterns.why: A messy wall of tasks is something every content team recognises, and a single action word ('rank', 'sort') promises order in one move. It reframes growth as using what you already have, which feels cheaper than starting over.
patterns.picture: Many small hand-drawn cards or notes scattered across the frame, with one bold action caption, then they start to line up. For Floey: a garden full of flowers, each with a tiny tag, rearranging into a row with the ones closest to page one at the front.
patterns.forFlowra: Your next traffic win is a page you already published.

examples.words: On screen: 'RANK BY IMPACT,' (title: 'How to Turn Existing Website Traffic Into More Revenue | CRO & Experimentation')
examples.onScreen: Cover only: hand-drawn coloured sticky notes with tiny charts scattered on a white wall, bold white caption

patterns.name: Two counters, side by side
patterns.formula: Your [usual approach] versus [the overlooked one], shown side by side.
patterns.why: Two counters placed next to each other ask the eye to compare straight away, and the gap between them is the hook before a word is spoken. This is weak evidence, from a single low-scoring cover.
patterns.picture: Two labelled counters or bars at the top of the frame with a face or character pointing up at them. For Floey: two flowers labelled 'before' and 'after' with bars filling up, with no figures shown unless they are a real measured result.
patterns.forFlowra: Your page before the change and after it, side by side, adjusted for the whole site.

examples.words: On screen: '1,125 Hastage' and '308K keyword' (title: '| Instagram SEO | Instagram Keywords | Reels Growth Tips')
examples.onScreen: Cover only: young man holding a mic, finger raised, two view counters above his head comparing hashtag and keyword

avoid: A slow start before the problem (a logo, an establishing shot of the garden, Floey flying in). Our own early signal is that Instagram viewers leave within the first few seconds, so the problem has to be on screen and spoken in frame one.

Using one opening for every platform without checking. In our four reels the problem reel led on Instagram while the news reels (especially r004) did better on YouTube. That is an early signal from one snapshot, so test problem-led and news-led openings on both platforms before choosing.
Greetings and self-introductions ('Hi, I'm Floey'). They break the house rules and waste the 2 seconds a hook has to land.
Yes or no questions copied from strangers' titles ('Can your website handle the traffic?'). The viewer can answer 'yes' and scroll away. Restate them as a specific claim about the viewer's site.

Hype numbers and invented counters ('Drive millions', 'Rank and scale faster', made-up figures on before and after bars). They are invented results that break our rule on statistics and promise outcomes Flowra can't back.

Indexing promises like the SpeedyIndex reels make. Flowra asks Google to recrawl on publish and monitors index coverage, but it never guarantees indexing, so the 'without the usual chore' pattern must never promise that.

Walls of thumbnail text (several badges, checklists, 'FULL GUIDE'). These covers are thumbnails, not real opening frames, and nobody can read that much in a 25 to 45 second animation. Use one line, at most two.
Long tutorial setups (the 109 to 179 second videos). Their covers promise step-by-step lessons, which doesn't suit Flowra's short reels. Open on the single loss, not the course outline.

Treating these patterns as proven. For the second week running every example is cover only, with no spoken openings, and the top scorer is an off-topic Hindi AI video tutorial. Treat them as structures to test against our own reels.
